hydrogen-fuel-cell-s1.title: Two ways to drive on electricity

table.caption: Efficiency of each step from electricity on the grid to energy at a car's wheels (invented data for practice, near published estimates)

hydrogen-fuel-cell-s2.title: How a hydrogen fuel cell works

items.q: What is the only exhaust from a hydrogen fuel cell?
options: Carbon dioxide
Methane
Soot
Water

why.correct: Hydrogen combines with oxygen from the air: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The product is water (and some heat).
options: The fuel contains no carbon, so the cell makes no carbon dioxide.
Methane is not produced in the cell.
Nothing is burned, so there is no soot.
Right: water is the product.

items.q: How does a hydrogen fuel cell differ from burning hydrogen?
options: It splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight
It stores electricity from the grid in a chemical battery
It makes electricity from a reaction, with no flame
It burns hydrogen in a flame to boil water for a turbine

why.correct: In a fuel cell the reaction happens across a membrane, and the electrons that move through an outside circuit are the electric current. There is no combustion.
options: Splitting water uses electricity; it is the reverse of a fuel cell.
A fuel cell makes electricity from fuel; it does not store grid electricity.
Right: a chemical reaction makes electricity directly.
A fuel cell has no flame and no turbine.

items.q: Most hydrogen produced today comes from natural gas. What does this mean for a fuel cell car's environmental impact?
options: The car releases methane from its fuel cell as it drives along
Carbon dioxide is released at the plant that makes hydrogen
The car releases carbon dioxide out of its exhaust pipe
The car is zero emissions from start to finish, at each step

why.correct: Steam reforming of natural gas releases carbon dioxide at the plant. A fuel cell vehicle is only as clean as the way its hydrogen is made.
options: The fuel cell uses hydrogen, not methane.
Right: the emissions move to the hydrogen plant.
The car's exhaust is water.
Making the hydrogen from natural gas releases carbon dioxide.

items.q: Which drawback belongs to hydrogen fuel cell cars rather than battery-powered cars?
options: Few fueling stations, and hydrogen is hard to store
Long recharging times at home or at public charging stations
Large batteries that need mined lithium, cobalt and nickel
Driving range that falls sharply in very cold winter weather

why.correct: Fuel cell cars refuel in minutes, but hydrogen is hard to store and move, and there are very few stations. Long charging times and large mined batteries are battery-car drawbacks.
options: Right: hydrogen storage and the lack of stations.
Long recharging is a battery car drawback; fuel cell cars refuel in minutes.
Large lithium batteries are a battery car drawback; fuel cell cars have only a small battery.
Cold weather mainly cuts the range of battery cars.

items.q: Why is hydrogen called an energy carrier rather than an energy source?
options: It carries electric current through the power lines
It is found in large underground deposits, like natural gas
It releases more energy in the cell than it took to make
Energy must be used to make it, and it then carries that energy

why.correct: Hydrogen is bound up in water and hydrocarbons. Making it (by electrolysis or from natural gas) takes energy, which the hydrogen then carries to the fuel cell, with losses.
options: Hydrogen is a gas fuel, not electric current.
Free hydrogen is very rare in nature.
Making hydrogen takes more energy than the fuel cell gets back.
Right: it stores energy that came from another source.

items.q: Hydrogen made by electrolysis using electricity from the wind is sometimes called "green hydrogen." What is its main advantage?
options: It needs no storage, since it is used as soon as it is made
It makes the wind-driven generators more efficient
Very little carbon dioxide is released at any step
It costs less to make than hydrogen made from natural gas

why.correct: With renewable electricity, splitting water releases no carbon dioxide, so the whole chain is very low in emissions. It is currently more expensive than hydrogen from gas.
options: It still needs storage and transport.
Making hydrogen does not change turbine efficiency.
Right: the whole chain is very low carbon.
Today it costs more than hydrogen from natural gas.

items.q: What is the overall efficiency of path A, from the electricity used to make hydrogen to the energy that turns the car's wheels? Give a percent.

mistakes.why: You averaged the four steps. Losses build on each other, so multiply the efficiencies: 0.70 × 0.85 × 0.50 × 0.90.
That is the efficiency as a decimal. Multiply by 100 for a percent.

items.q: What is the overall efficiency of path B, the battery-powered car? Give a percent.

mistakes.why: You averaged the three steps. Multiply them: 0.92 × 0.95 × 0.90.

items.q: A fuel cell car needs 20 kWh at its wheels for a trip. Write the setup for the electricity that must go into path A to make the hydrogen, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Multiplying finds what comes out. Here 20 kWh is the output, so divide by the efficiency to find the input.
Put the whole product of efficiencies in brackets: 20 ÷ (0.70 × 0.85 × 0.50 × 0.90).
You found the output from 20 kWh of input. The 20 kWh is the output here, so divide.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: The two paths deliver about the same share of energy to the wheels
The fuel cell step is the most efficient of the steps in path A
Path B goes about three times as far on the same electricity
The fuel cell path wastes less energy than the battery path does

why.correct: Path B delivers about 78.7 percent and path A about 26.8 percent, roughly three times as much, so the same electricity goes about three times as far.
options: About 27 percent against about 79 percent is a big gap.
The fuel cell, at 50 percent, is the least efficient step in path A.
Path A wastes about 73 percent; path B about 21 percent.

items.q: In the diagram, what passes through the membrane?
options: Water
Hydrogen ions
Electrons
Oxygen gas

why.correct: The membrane lets hydrogen ions (H⁺) through but blocks electrons, which must go around through the circuit.
options: Water forms at the cathode and leaves the cell.
Right: H⁺ ions cross the membrane.
Electrons are forced through the outside circuit, which is the current.
Oxygen enters at the cathode from the air.

items.q: According to the diagram, why does the motor run?
options: Electrons flow through the outside circuit as a current
Oxygen burns at the cathode, which spins the motor
Water leaving the cell turns a small turbine inside it
Hydrogen ions push on the motor as they cross the membrane

why.correct: The membrane blocks electrons, so they travel through the outside circuit from anode to cathode. That flow is the electric current that runs the motor.
options: Right: the electron flow is the current.
Nothing burns in a fuel cell.
There is no turbine in a fuel cell.
The ions stay inside the cell; the current is the electrons.

items.q: A city replaces diesel buses with fuel cell buses like the one in the diagram. Which air quality change on city streets is most likely?
options: More carbon dioxide on the streets released by the fuel cells
More soot, since hydrogen burns at a very high temperature
No change, since the new buses still burn fuel in their engines
Less soot and exhaust on the streets, as the buses emit water

why.correct: The buses emit only water vapor, so street-level exhaust from the buses falls. Emissions may still occur where the hydrogen is made.
options: Fuel cells emit no carbon dioxide.
Nothing is burned in a fuel cell.
Fuel cells do not burn fuel.
Right: tailpipe pollution from the buses goes away.

items.q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of the fuel cell buses, compared with diesel buses.

why.correct: Advantage: no harmful exhaust, only water. Disadvantage: making hydrogen takes energy, often from natural gas, and storing and supplying it is costly.

specific.frame: An advantage is that ___. A disadvantage is that ___.

adv.label: Advantage
options: the buses release only water, so street-level air pollution falls
hydrogen is free and found in large deposits
the buses need no fueling at all

why.1: Hydrogen must be made using energy; it is not mined.
why.2: The buses must be refueled with hydrogen.

dis.label: Disadvantage
options: making hydrogen takes energy, often from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide
the buses release soot from their exhaust
the buses need long battery recharges each night

why.2: Long recharging is a battery bus drawback; fuel cell buses refuel in minutes.

specific.model: An advantage is that the buses release only water, so street-level air pollution falls because no diesel is burned. A disadvantage is that making hydrogen takes energy, often from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide at the plant.

items.q: Which is an advantage of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles over battery-powered cars?
options: Their fuel is cheaper to make and easier to store safely
They refuel in a few minutes and go a long way per fill
They have many more fueling stations available to drivers
They use energy more efficiently from the source to the wheels

why.correct: Fuel cell vehicles refuel quickly and have long range, which suits trucks and buses. They are less efficient overall, and hydrogen is costly and hard to store.
options: Hydrogen is costly and must be stored under high pressure or very cold.
Right: fast refueling and long range.
Hydrogen stations are rare.
The battery path is about three times as efficient.

items.q: What does electrolysis do in the hydrogen fuel chain?
options: Uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen
Combines hydrogen and oxygen to make electricity
Burns hydrogen in a flame to boil water for steam
Separates hydrogen from natural gas using hot steam

why.correct: Electrolysis runs electricity through water to split it. It is the reverse of what a fuel cell does.
options: Right: electricity splits water.
That is what the fuel cell does.
Hydrogen is not burned in this chain.
That is steam reforming of natural gas.
